items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Nina Ortega, a cash-basis taxpayer, received the following amounts in 2026. Which amount must she include in gross income?
options: A $4,000 cash gift from her aunt
$150,000 of life insurance proceeds paid on the death of her father
$1,200 of interest on a bond issued by her home state's water authority
$3,000 of unemployment compensation paid by her state

why.A: Gifts are excluded from the recipient's gross income. The donor may owe gift tax, but the recipient does not report the gift.
why.B: Life insurance proceeds paid by reason of the insured's death are excluded, unless the policy was transferred for value, which is not the case here.
why.C: Interest on state and local government bonds is excluded from regular gross income.
why.D: Unemployment compensation is taxable income and is reported on Schedule 1, even though it is a government benefit and not pay for services.

items.rule_line: Unemployment compensation is taxable; gifts, life insurance proceeds and state or local bond interest are excluded.

guide.ask: Which receipts are excluded from gross income by statute?
guide.reveal: Gifts, life insurance death proceeds, and state and local bond interest.

guide.ask: Which listed receipt has no exclusion even though it is a government benefit?
guide.reveal: Unemployment compensation, which is taxable.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Leo Brandt earned $58,000 of salary in 2026. His employer also paid $7,000 of his graduate tuition under a written educational assistance program that meets all legal requirements and allows up to $5,250 per year to be excluded. What total amount of these items is included in Leo's gross income?

why.A: Subtracts the exclusion from salary. The exclusion applies to the tuition benefit, and the salary is fully taxable.
why.B: Excludes the entire $7,000 of tuition. The exclusion stops at $5,250, so $1,750 is taxable.
why.C: Employer educational assistance is excluded only up to $5,250. The $1,750 excess is wages: $58,000 + ($7,000 - $5,250) = $59,750.
why.D: Includes the full tuition benefit and ignores the $5,250 exclusion for educational assistance programs.

items.rule_line: Employer educational assistance is excluded only up to $5,250 per year; the excess is wages.

guide.ask: Is the salary fully included?
How much tuition assistance is excluded and how much is included?
guide.reveal: Exclusion capped at 5,250, so 7,000 - 5,250 = 1,750 is wages.

guide.ask: What is the total?

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Sam Whitfield is a partner in Whitfield & Cole, a calendar-year partnership. For 2026 the partnership paid Sam $40,000 for services, determined without regard to partnership income. Sam's share of partnership ordinary income, after all partnership deductions including that payment, was $15,000. The partnership also distributed $30,000 in cash to Sam during the year. Assume Sam's basis in his partnership interest is sufficient to absorb the distribution. What amount does Sam include in gross income from the partnership for 2026?

why.A: Counts only the guaranteed payment. The partner is also taxed on the distributive share of partnership income.
why.B: The guaranteed payment ($40,000) is ordinary income to Sam. His distributive share ($15,000) is taxed whether or not it is distributed. The $30,000 cash distribution is a return of basis, not income.
why.C: Adds the cash distribution to the guaranteed payment. A distribution is not income unless it exceeds the partner's basis.
why.D: Also adds the $30,000 distribution. Distributions reduce basis; only the guaranteed payment and the distributive share are taxed.

steps: Distributive share 15,000 (taxed as earned by the partnership)
Cash distribution 30,000 is not income (basis recovery)
items.rule_line: A partner is taxed on guaranteed payments and the distributive share; cash distributions reduce basis and are not income.

guide.ask: How is the guaranteed payment treated?
guide.reveal: Ordinary income of 40,000.

guide.ask: What about the distributive share and the cash distribution?
guide.reveal: The 15,000 share is taxed as earned; the 30,000 distribution is a basis recovery, not income.

guide.ask: What is the total?

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be excluded from an individual's gross income (tax-exempt interest, gifts received, life insurance proceeds).
items.stem: Maria Santos received $900 of interest from a savings account, $1,100 of interest on an Ohio school district bond, and $1,500 of interest on a qualified private activity bond issued by an Ohio airport authority. The private activity bond interest is exempt from regular income tax but is an AMT preference item. What amount of interest is included in Maria's 2026 regular taxable income?

why.A: Only the bank interest is taxable. Interest on state and local bonds, including qualified private activity bonds, is excluded for regular tax; the private activity bond interest matters only for the AMT.
why.B: Includes the school district bond interest. Interest on state and local government bonds is excluded from gross income.
why.C: Includes the private activity bond interest. It is excluded from regular tax and is only a preference item for the AMT.
why.D: Treats all interest as taxable. Bank interest is taxable, but interest on state and local bonds is excluded.

steps: School district bond interest 1,100 is excluded
Private activity bond interest 1,500 is excluded for regular tax (AMT preference)
items.rule_line: Interest on state and local bonds, including private activity bonds, is excluded from regular income; private activity bond interest is only an AMT preference.

guide.ask: Which of the three interest items is taxable for regular tax?
guide.reveal: Only the bank interest of 900.

guide.ask: What about the school district bond and the private activity bond?
guide.reveal: Both are excluded for regular tax; the private activity bond is only an AMT preference item.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Rina Kapoor, age 68, began receiving $800 per month from a commercial annuity in 2025. She bought the annuity with $48,000 of after-tax money, and her expected return under the IRS tables is $80,000. She received $9,600 during 2026. What amount of the 2026 payments is included in gross income?

why.A: Treats all payments as a recovery of her $48,000 investment first. That basis-first rule applies only to annuities that started before 1987.
why.C: This is the excluded portion ($5,760), not the taxable portion.
why.D: Treats every payment as taxable. Part of each payment is a tax-free return of the after-tax investment.

items.rule_line: An annuity's taxable part is the payment less the exclusion ratio of investment divided by expected return.

guide.ask: What is the exclusion ratio?
How much of the 9,600 is excluded?
What is taxable?

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Robert Hale, a single taxpayer, received $20,000 of Social Security benefits in 2026. His other income included in AGI was $30,000, and he also received $2,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest. What amount of his Social Security benefits is included in gross income?

why.A: Applies 85% only to provisional income above $34,000 and omits the first tier of $4,500 taxed at 50%.
why.B: Includes just 50% of benefits, which is the maximum only when provisional income is between the $25,000 and $34,000 base amounts.
why.C: Provisional income = $30,000 + $2,000 + 50% x $20,000 = $42,000. Above $34,000 the taxable amount is the lesser of 85% of benefits or: lesser of 50% of benefits or $4,500, plus 85% x ($42,000 - $34,000) = $4,500 + $6,800 = $11,300.
why.D: Includes the maximum 85%. His provisional income is not high enough to reach the 85% cap.

items.rule_line: Social Security benefits are taxable up to 85% based on provisional income and the $25,000 and $34,000 base amounts.

guide.ask: What is provisional income?
What is the first-tier amount for a single filer and the second tier?
What is the taxable benefit?

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Dan Roe's credit card issuer canceled $20,000 of his debt in 2026 and issued a Form 1099-C. Immediately before the cancellation, Dan's liabilities totaled $162,000 and the fair market value of his assets totaled $150,000. Dan was not in bankruptcy. What amount of canceled debt must Dan include in 2026 gross income?

why.A: Excludes the entire $20,000. The insolvency exclusion is limited to the amount by which liabilities exceed the fair market value of assets ($12,000).
why.B: Canceled debt is income unless an exclusion applies. Dan was insolvent by $12,000 immediately before the cancellation, so he may exclude up to $12,000. Income = $20,000 - $12,000 = $8,000.
why.C: This is the amount of the insolvency, which is the excluded amount, not the amount included.
why.D: Includes the full canceled amount and ignores the insolvency exclusion.

items.rule_line: Canceled debt is income except to the extent of insolvency immediately before cancellation.

guide.ask: What is Dan's insolvency amount?
How much may be excluded?
guide.reveal: The lesser of 20,000 canceled or 12,000 insolvency, so 12,000.

guide.ask: What is included?

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be excluded from an individual's gross income (tax-exempt interest, gifts received, life insurance proceeds).
items.stem: Which of the following amounts received in settlement of a lawsuit may be excluded from the recipient's gross income?
options: Punitive damages awarded in the same physical injury case
Back pay received in an employment discrimination settlement
Damages for emotional distress from a defamation claim with no physical injury
Compensatory damages for medical costs and pain caused by a physical injury in a car accident

why.A: Punitive damages are taxable, even when the underlying claim is for a physical injury.
why.B: Back pay replaces wages and is taxable as wages, not as damages for physical injury.
why.C: Emotional distress is not a physical injury. Such damages are taxable, except for the amount that reimburses medical care for the distress.
why.D: Damages received on account of personal physical injury or physical sickness are excluded, whether received as a lump sum or as periodic payments.

items.rule_line: Damages for personal physical injury or sickness are excluded; punitive, back pay and non-physical emotional distress damages are taxable.

guide.ask: Which settlement amounts are excluded?
guide.reveal: Damages received on account of personal physical injury or physical sickness.

guide.ask: Which listed receipt is that?
guide.reveal: Compensatory damages for medical costs and pain from a car-accident injury; punitive, back pay and non-physical emotional distress are taxable.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Kay Morgan was seriously injured in a collision with a delivery truck. In 2026 she received a judgment of $100,000 consisting of $60,000 compensatory damages for her physical injuries, $25,000 punitive damages, and $15,000 of interest on the judgment. What amount must Kay include in gross income for 2026?

why.A: Includes only the interest. Punitive damages are also taxable.
why.B: Includes only punitive damages. Interest on a judgment is taxable as well.
why.C: Compensatory damages for physical injury are excluded. Punitive damages ($25,000) and interest on the judgment ($15,000) are taxable: $40,000.
why.D: Includes the compensatory damages, which are excluded because they are received on account of physical injury.

items.rule_line: Compensatory damages for physical injury are excluded, but punitive damages and interest on the judgment are taxable.

guide.ask: Which parts of the judgment are excluded?
guide.reveal: Compensatory damages for physical injury, 60,000.

guide.ask: Which parts are taxable?
guide.reveal: Punitive damages 25,000 and interest 15,000.

guide.ask: What is the total inclusion?

items.task: Calculate the capital gain included in gross income from sale of investments/virtual currency, gifts and inherited assets; classify as long-term or short-term.
items.stem: Ken Ruiz bought 500 shares of stock on January 20, 2025 for $20,000 and sold all of the shares on March 25, 2026 for $28,000. How should Ken report the sale?
options: An $8,000 short-term capital gain
An $8,000 ordinary gain
A $28,000 long-term capital gain
An $8,000 long-term capital gain

why.A: Short-term applies only to a holding period of one year or less. Ken held the shares for about 14 months.
why.B: Gain on investment stock is a capital gain, not ordinary income.
why.C: Uses the sales price as the gain. Gain is the amount realized less adjusted basis.
why.D: Ken held the shares for more than one year (about 14 months), so the $8,000 gain ($28,000 - $20,000) is long-term.

items.rule_line: Stock held more than one year produces long-term capital gain equal to amount realized less basis.

guide.ask: How long was the stock held?
guide.reveal: From January 20, 2025 to March 25, 2026, more than a year.

guide.ask: What is the gain and its character?

items.task: Calculate the capital gain included in gross income from sale of investments/virtual currency, gifts and inherited assets; classify as long-term or short-term.
items.stem: Alicia Torres inherited 300 shares of stock when her uncle died on June 1, 2026. Her uncle's basis was $12,000, and the shares were worth $50,000 on the date of death. Alicia sold all of the shares on August 15, 2026 for $54,000. How should she report the sale?
options: A $4,000 short-term capital gain
A $42,000 long-term capital gain
A $42,000 short-term capital gain
A $4,000 long-term capital gain

why.A: Uses the right gain but the wrong holding period. Property acquired from a decedent is automatically long-term.
why.B: Uses the uncle's $12,000 basis. Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to fair market value at death.
why.C: Makes both errors: it carries over the decedent's basis and treats the holding period as only a few months.
why.D: Inherited property takes the date-of-death value ($50,000) as basis and is treated as long-term regardless of how long the heir held it: $54,000 - $50,000 = $4,000 long-term.

items.rule_line: Inherited property takes FMV at death as basis and is automatically long-term.

guide.ask: What basis does an heir take?
guide.reveal: Date-of-death value, 50,000.

guide.ask: What is the holding period treatment?
guide.reveal: Long-term regardless of how long the heir held it.

guide.ask: What is the result?

items.task: Calculate the capital gain included in gross income from sale of investments/virtual currency, gifts and inherited assets; classify as long-term or short-term.
items.stem: Wen Zhao received 1,000 shares of stock as a gift from her father in 2026. Her father's adjusted basis was $50,000, and the fair market value on the gift date was $30,000. No gift tax was paid. Wen later sold all the shares in 2026 for $26,000. What loss does Wen recognize on the sale?

why.A: For a loss, the donee's basis is the lower of the donor's basis or fair market value at the gift date: $30,000. Loss = $30,000 - $26,000 = $4,000.
why.B: This is the built-in loss ($20,000) at the gift date, which stays with the donor's basis and is never recognized by the donee.
why.C: Uses the donor's $50,000 basis. That carryover basis applies only for computing gain, not loss, when value has declined.
why.D: Reports the entire sale price as the loss. The loss is the basis, as limited, less the amount realized.

steps: Sale price 26,000 is below FMV at gift 30,000 and below donor basis 50,000
items.rule_line: A donee's loss basis is the lower of the donor's basis or FMV at the gift date.

guide.ask: Which basis applies to a loss on gift property when FMV is below the donor's basis?
guide.reveal: The lower of the donor's basis or FMV at the gift date, 30,000.

guide.ask: What is the loss?

items.task: Calculate the capital gain included in gross income from sale of investments/virtual currency, gifts and inherited assets; classify as long-term or short-term.
items.stem: Bea Lindgren bought 2 units of a virtual currency for $10,000 in total ($5,000 each) in 2025. In 2026, when one unit was worth $9,000, she used that unit to buy furniture for her home. What gain must Bea report on the transaction?

why.A: There is no exception for using virtual currency on personal purchases. The disposition is taxable even though the furniture is personal.
why.B: Virtual currency is property. Paying for a personal purchase with it is a sale or exchange: amount realized $9,000 less basis $5,000 = $4,000 long-term gain (held over one year).
why.C: Reports the cost of the unit as the gain. Gain is the value received less the cost.
why.D: Reports the value received as gain and ignores the $5,000 basis in the unit used.

steps: Amount realized = fair market value of the unit, 9,000
items.rule_line: Paying for a personal purchase with virtual currency is a taxable disposition of property; gain is value received less basis.

guide.ask: What is virtual currency for tax purposes and what is the basis of the unit spent?
What is the amount realized in buying furniture?
guide.reveal: The unit's FMV, 9,000.

guide.ask: What is the gain and its character?

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be excluded from an individual's gross income (tax-exempt interest, gifts received, life insurance proceeds).
items.stem: Marta Ibarra inherited a duplex from her aunt in 2026. The duplex was worth $300,000 on the date of death. Marta rented it out and collected $8,000 of rent for the rest of the year. Ignore any rental deductions. What amount does Marta include in 2026 gross income for the duplex?

why.A: Excludes the rent too. Only the inheritance itself is excluded; later income from the property is taxable.
why.B: Property received by inheritance is excluded from gross income, but income the property later produces, such as rent, is taxable: $8,000.
why.C: Includes the value of the inherited property, which is excluded from gross income.
why.D: Includes both the inheritance and the rent. The inheritance is excluded.

items.rule_line: Inheritance is excluded from gross income, but rent the inherited property produces afterward is taxable.

guide.ask: Is inherited property itself income?
guide.reveal: No, it is excluded.

guide.ask: Is the rent it produces income?
guide.reveal: Yes, the 8,000 of rent is taxable.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be excluded from an individual's gross income (tax-exempt interest, gifts received, life insurance proceeds).
items.stem: Carla Denton's father died in 2026. Carla, the beneficiary of his $90,000 life insurance policy, chose to receive the proceeds in ten equal annual installments of $10,000. The insurer credits extra amounts, which are the interest, so each installment is $1,000 more than one-tenth of the proceeds. She received the first installment in 2026. What amount must Carla include in gross income for 2026?

why.A: Excludes the interest. Life insurance proceeds are excluded, but interest earned on proceeds held by the insurer is taxable.
why.B: The proration excludes $9,000 of each installment as death benefit. The $1,000 extra is interest and is taxable.
why.C: Includes the death benefit part and excludes the interest, which reverses the rule.
why.D: Includes the whole installment. Only the interest element is taxable.

items.rule_line: Life insurance proceeds are excluded, but interest added to installment payments is taxable.

guide.ask: How much of each installment is the excluded death benefit?
What is the interest element in the first installment?
What is included in 2026?

items.task: Calculate the income reported in the year of death for a decedent.
items.stem: Ed Marlow, a cash-basis taxpayer, died on September 30, 2026. Through that date he had received $70,000 of salary. In November 2026, his employer paid Ed's estate $6,000 of wages that Ed had earned but had not been paid before death. What amount of these items is reported on Ed's final Form 1040 for 2026?

why.A: Reports nothing, but the $70,000 of salary already received is income on the final return.
why.B: Reports only the unpaid wages. Those are income in respect of a decedent taxed to the estate, not to Ed.
why.C: A cash-basis decedent reports only income actually or constructively received before death: $70,000. The $6,000 is income in respect of a decedent, taxed to the estate or heir who receives it.
why.D: Accrues the $6,000 on the final return. A cash-basis decedent does not report income received after death.

steps: Wages paid after death = income in respect of a decedent (estate or heir reports 6,000)
items.rule_line: A cash-basis decedent's final return reports only income received before death; later wages are income in respect of a decedent taxed to the recipient.

guide.ask: What does a cash-basis decedent's final return report?
guide.reveal: Income actually or constructively received before death, 70,000.

guide.ask: How is the later wage payment classified?
guide.reveal: Income in respect of a decedent, reported by the estate or heir, so 6,000 stays off the final return.

items.task: Calculate the income reported in the year of death for a decedent.
items.stem: Frank Tull, a cash-basis taxpayer, sold land he had held as an investment for four years under an installment sale and reported long-term capital gain on the payments he received. He died before collecting the last installment, and his estate collected it. How does the estate treat the gain in that installment?
options: As ordinary income, because it is income in respect of a decedent
As short-term capital gain, because the estate held the note only a short time
As excluded income, because the note received a stepped-up basis at death
As long-term capital gain, the same character it would have had in Frank's hands

why.A: IRD is not automatically ordinary. Its character follows the character it would have had for the decedent.
why.B: The estate does not restart the holding period. The character is determined as if the decedent had received the payment.
why.C: Installment notes are IRD assets and do not get a basis step-up. The estate or heir reports the gain as it is collected.
why.D: Income in respect of a decedent keeps the character it would have had if the decedent had lived, so the installment gain remains long-term capital gain.

items.rule_line: Income in respect of a decedent keeps the character it would have had for the decedent and gets no basis step-up.

guide.ask: What is the installment note gain when collected by an estate called?
guide.reveal: Income in respect of a decedent.

guide.ask: What character does it keep?
guide.reveal: The character it would have had for the decedent, so long-term capital gain.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Gina Pratt divorced in 2022 under a decree that requires her former spouse to pay $1,500 per month of alimony and $800 per month of child support. She received all payments in 2026. What amount of these payments is included in Gina's 2026 gross income?

why.A: For divorce instruments executed after 2018, alimony is neither deductible by the payer nor included in the recipient's income. Child support is never income. Neither payment is included.
why.B: Includes only the child support. Child support is never included in the recipient's income.
why.C: Includes the alimony as under pre-2019 divorce rules. Alimony under a post-2018 instrument is not taxable to the recipient.
why.D: Includes both payments. Neither alimony under a post-2018 instrument nor child support is income to the recipient.

steps: Decree date 2022 = after 2018: alimony not included
items.rule_line: For divorce instruments after 2018, alimony is not income to the recipient, and child support never is.

guide.ask: Is alimony taxable under a decree executed after 2018?
guide.reveal: No, neither deductible by the payer nor income to the recipient.

guide.ask: What about child support?
guide.reveal: Never income, so the included amount is 0.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Hal Perez, a plumber, repaired the pipes in a dentist's office in 2026 in exchange for dental work. Both services would normally cost $1,200. What amount must Hal include in gross income from the exchange?

why.A: No cash changed hands, but barter income is taxable at the fair market value of what is received.
why.B: Splits the value between the two parties. Each party reports the full value of what he receives.
why.C: Bartering creates income equal to the fair market value of the property or services received: $1,200.
why.D: Adds the value of both services. Hal reports only the dental work he received.

items.rule_line: Bartering income equals the FMV of the property or services received.

guide.ask: Is barter income?
guide.reveal: Yes.

guide.ask: How is the amount measured?
guide.reveal: At the FMV of what is received, 1,200 of dental work.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be excluded from an individual's gross income (tax-exempt interest, gifts received, life insurance proceeds).
items.stem: Two students each received a $6,000 scholarship in 2026. Ann, a degree candidate at a university, used hers entirely for tuition and required books. Bob, also a degree candidate, used his entirely for room and board. What is the tax treatment of the two scholarships?
options: Both students exclude the full amount
Both students include the full amount
Ann includes hers; Bob excludes his
Ann excludes hers; Bob includes his

why.A: Room and board is a personal cost that is not a qualified education expense, so Bob's scholarship is taxable.
why.B: Ann's scholarship is used for qualified tuition and required books, so it is excluded.
why.C: Reverses the rule. Qualified education expenses are excluded; room and board is not.
why.D: A degree candidate excludes the part of a scholarship used for tuition, fees, books, and required supplies. Amounts used for room and board are taxable.

items.rule_line: Scholarship amounts used for tuition, fees, books and required supplies are excluded; amounts for room and board are taxable.

guide.ask: Which scholarship uses are excluded for a degree candidate?
guide.reveal: Tuition, fees, books and required supplies.

guide.ask: How do the two students' uses compare?
guide.reveal: Ann used it all for tuition and books, so she excludes it; Bob used it for room and board, so he includes it.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Priya, an employee, received two items from her employer in December 2026. First, a $100 holiday turkey given to all employees. Second, a $100 gift card redeemable at any store, also given to all employees. How should Priya treat the items?
options: Both items are excluded as de minimis fringe benefits
Both items are included in wages
The gift card is excluded and the turkey is included in wages
The turkey is excluded as a de minimis fringe benefit; the gift card is included in wages

why.A: Cash equivalents, including general-use gift cards, are always taxable regardless of amount.
why.B: The turkey is a small item of property that is difficult to account for, so it qualifies as a de minimis fringe benefit.
why.C: Reverses the rule. Cash equivalents are taxable; occasional low-value property is not.
why.D: Occasional low-value property such as a holiday turkey is a de minimis fringe benefit. Cash and cash equivalents such as general gift cards are never de minimis and are taxable wages.

items.rule_line: Occasional low-value property is a de minimis fringe benefit, but cash and cash equivalents such as general gift cards are taxable wages.

guide.ask: What makes a fringe benefit de minimis?
guide.reveal: Occasional, low-value property or services that are hard to account for.

guide.ask: Which item can never be de minimis?
guide.reveal: Cash and cash equivalents such as a general gift card, which are taxable wages; the holiday turkey is de minimis.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Which of the following is included in the gross income of an individual who receives it in 2026?
options: A $2,500 birthday gift from a grandparent
A $2,500 inheritance from a great-aunt's will
A $2,500 reimbursement of an employee's business travel under an accountable plan
A $2,500 prize won on a television game show

why.A: Gifts are excluded from the recipient's gross income.
why.B: Property received by inheritance is excluded from gross income.
why.C: Reimbursements under an accountable plan are not wages and are excluded.
why.D: Prizes and awards, including game show winnings, are included in gross income at fair market value.

items.rule_line: Prizes and game show winnings are included in gross income, while gifts, inheritances and accountable plan reimbursements are excluded.

guide.ask: Which receipts are excluded?
guide.reveal: Gifts, inheritances, and accountable plan reimbursements.

guide.ask: Which receipt is a prize with no exclusion?
guide.reveal: The game show prize, included at FMV.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Owen Blake, a cash-basis taxpayer, receives a $5,000 bonus on January 3, 2027 for work performed in 2026. The bonus check was available to him on December 30, 2026 in his employer's payroll office, but Owen chose not to pick it up until January 3. In which year is the bonus income?
options: 2027, because Owen did not receive the check until January 3
2026 and 2027, split equally, because the work was in 2026 and payment in 2027
2027, because the bonus was earned by services performed in 2026
2026, because the bonus was constructively received when it was made available

why.A: A cash-basis taxpayer cannot postpone income by choosing not to collect an amount that is available to him.
why.B: Income is not allocated by service period. It is reported in the year actually or constructively received.
why.C: The year the work was performed is irrelevant to a cash-basis taxpayer. Receipt controls.
why.D: Under constructive receipt, a cash-basis taxpayer reports income when it is credited or set apart and available without substantial restriction, even if he does not take possession.

items.rule_line: A cash-basis taxpayer reports income when it is constructively received, meaning available without substantial restriction.

He reports it as a long-term capital gain, because virtual currency is property
He reports it as wages subject to withholding, because the customer is an employer
He reports the fair market value in U.S. dollars of the currency, on the date received, as self-employment income

why.B: Uses the father's original basis as the difference. The gap is the appreciation before the transfer ($60,000 - $20,000 = $40,000).
why.C: Aaron takes the donor's $20,000 basis: gain $45,000. Bella takes the date-of-death value: gain $5,000. The difference is $40,000.
why.D: Adds the two gains instead of subtracting them.

items.stem: Compare two taxpayers in 2026. Anna has $20,000 of credit card debt canceled while her liabilities exceed the value of her assets by $30,000 immediately before the cancellation. Ben has $20,000 of credit card debt canceled while he is solvent, with assets exceeding liabilities by $50,000 immediately before the cancellation. Neither is in bankruptcy. Which statement is correct?

Anna includes $10,000 and Ben includes $20,000
Both include the entire $20,000, because neither filed for bankruptcy
Anna excludes the entire $20,000; Ben includes the entire $20,000

why.A: Consumer debt receives no special exclusion. Cancellation is income unless an exclusion such as insolvency applies.
why.B: Anna's exclusion is limited by her insolvency of $30,000, which is greater than the $20,000 canceled, so she includes nothing.
why.C: Bankruptcy is only one exclusion. Insolvency outside bankruptcy also allows an exclusion up to the amount of insolvency.
why.D: Anna's insolvency ($30,000) is at least as large as the canceled debt, so all $20,000 is excluded. Ben is solvent and has no exclusion, so he has $20,000 of ordinary income.

items.rule_line: Canceled debt is excludable to the extent of insolvency immediately before cancellation; a solvent debtor includes it all.

guide.ask: How much cancelled debt may an insolvent taxpayer exclude?
guide.reveal: Up to the amount of insolvency.

guide.ask: How do the two compare?
guide.reveal: Anna's 30,000 insolvency covers all 20,000, so she excludes it; Ben is solvent and includes all 20,000.

options: The $9,000 interest should be added to the final return, because it accrued before death
The $18,000 of pension distributions received before death should be removed from the final return
The final return must be filed as married filing separately because Walter died
The $9,000 interest is correctly excluded from the final return, and the estate reports it when collected

why.D: Interest that a cash-basis decedent had earned but not received before death is income in respect of a decedent. It is reported by the person who receives it.

why.C: Uses the fraction of basis already recovered ($12,000 / $30,000) as the ratio. The exclusion ratio is total contributions over expected return.

why.D: Adds the nondeductible expenses instead of subtracting them.

His share of Alder's 2026 ordinary loss is $13,000. Ignoring the at-risk, passive activity, and excess business loss rules, what loss may Dario deduct on his 2026 return?

why.A: Denies the loss entirely. He has $8,000 of basis, so the loss is deductible up to that amount.
why.B: This is the suspended portion ($5,000), not the deductible amount.
why.C: A shareholder may deduct S corporation losses only up to his stock basis plus basis in loans to the corporation. With $8,000 of basis and no loan basis, he deducts $8,000. The remaining $5,000 is suspended and carried forward.
why.D: Deducts the full loss. The loss is limited to stock and debt basis.

steps: Deductible loss = lesser of loss 13,000 or basis 8,000 = 8,000

guide.ask: What limits a shareholder's S corporation loss deduction?
guide.reveal: Stock basis plus loan basis.

guide.ask: What is Dario's limit and what happens to the excess?
guide.reveal: 8,000, and the excess 5,000 is suspended and carried forward.

guide.reveal: The basis limitation.

guide.ask: What follows and what comes last?
guide.reveal: The at-risk rules, then the passive activity rules.

Ignoring income tax, the deduction for half of self-employment tax, and unemployment taxes, by how much does the S corporation structure reduce total Social Security and Medicare taxes, assuming all amounts are under the Social Security wage base?

why.A: This is the payroll tax on the salary, not the reduction. The savings equals the proprietor's tax less the S corporation payroll tax.
why.B: Sole proprietor: $100,000 x 92.35% x 15.3% = $14,130. S corporation: 15.3% (employer and employee shares) x $40,000 = $6,120. Difference: about $8,010.
why.C: Counts only the employee half of FICA on the salary and ignores the employer half, which the S corporation also owes.
why.D: Assumes the S corporation structure eliminates all employment tax. Wages of $40,000 are still subject to FICA.

items.rule_line: S corporation K-1 income is not subject to SE tax, but reasonable wages still bear FICA; savings equal the SE tax difference.

why.C: Long-term capital gain keeps its character and is reported on Schedule D.
why.D: A guaranteed payment for services is ordinary income to the partner and, for a general partner, is subject to self-employment tax. The draft return omits it.

items.stem: Two investors each contribute $10,000 to a venture. Priya invests as a general partner in a partnership that has $60,000 of recourse liabilities, of which $30,000 is allocated to her. Sam invests in an S corporation that has $60,000 of bank debt owed to unrelated lenders, and he has not loaned any money to the corporation. Each is allocated a $25,000 ordinary loss. Considering only the basis limitation, how much more of the loss can Priya deduct than Sam?

why.A: Assumes both use the same basis rules. Entity-level debt increases a partner's basis but not a shareholder's.
why.B: A partner's basis includes her share of partnership liabilities ($10,000 + $30,000 = $40,000), so Priya deducts the full $25,000. An S corporation shareholder's basis does not include corporate debt owed to others, so Sam deducts only $10,000. Difference: $15,000.
why.C: Treats Sam as deducting nothing. He can deduct losses up to his $10,000 stock basis.
why.D: Uses the liability share as the difference. Priya's deduction is capped at her $25,000 allocated loss.

items.rule_line: A partner's basis includes her share of partnership liabilities, but an S shareholder's basis excludes corporate debt owed to others.

guide.reveal: 10,000 + 30,000 of allocated recourse liabilities = 40,000, so she deducts the full 25,000.

guide.ask: What is Sam's basis?
guide.reveal: 10,000, since corporate debt owed to others does not add to it, so he deducts 10,000.

items.stem: Jon Pike has held stock in Pine Inc., an S corporation, for five years. After all 2026 income and loss adjustments, his stock basis before distributions was $22,000. $22,000 is a tax-free return of basis and $8,000 is ordinary dividend income
$22,000 is a tax-free return of basis and $8,000 is long-term capital gain
$30,000 is a long-term capital gain

why.A: Distributions reduce basis only to zero. The amount above basis is taxable gain.
why.B: With no accumulated earnings and profits there is no dividend. The excess is capital gain.
why.C: S corporation distributions with no earnings and profits are tax-free up to stock basis, and the excess is treated as gain from the sale of stock, here long-term.
why.D: Only the excess over basis ($8,000) is gain. The first $22,000 is a return of basis.

items.rule_line: S corporation distributions without E&P are tax-free up to stock basis, and the excess is capital gain.

guide.ask: How much of the 30,000 is tax-free?
guide.reveal: Up to stock basis, 22,000.

guide.ask: How is the excess treated with no earnings and profits?
guide.reveal: As gain from the sale of stock, long-term after five years, so 8,000 long-term capital gain.

why.B: Uses a $15,000 range instead of the $10,000 phase-out range.

why.D: Ignores the phase-out for a taxpayer covered by a workplace plan.

steps: Excess over the bottom of the range = 86,000 - 81,000 = 5,000

Carl's employer contributed $2,000 to his health savings account (HSA), and Carl contributed $9,000 of his own money. What HSA deduction may Carl claim?

why.A: The annual limit is $8,750 + $1,000 catch-up = $9,750, reduced by the $2,000 employer contribution: $7,750. The $1,250 excess of Carl's $9,000 is subject to the excess contribution tax unless withdrawn.
why.B: Uses the base family limit only, omitting the catch-up and the employer contribution.
why.C: Deducts the amount contributed without applying the limit.
why.D: Applies the $9,750 limit but does not subtract the $2,000 the employer already contributed.

items.rule_line: The HSA annual limit is the family limit plus catch-up if 55 or older, reduced by employer contributions.

guide.ask: What is Carl's annual limit including catch-up?
How does the employer contribution affect it?
What is the deduction?
guide.reveal: The lesser of 9,000 or 7,750, so 7,750, with the excess subject to tax unless withdrawn.

why.B: Individuals enrolled in Medicare cannot contribute to an HSA.
why.C: A person who can be claimed as a dependent by another taxpayer is not an eligible individual.
why.D: An eligible individual must have qualifying high-deductible health plan coverage, no other disqualifying health coverage, no Medicare enrollment, and not be claimable as a dependent.

why.A: SE tax = $80,000 x 92.35% x 15.3% = $11,303. The deduction is half of that, $5,652, and it is an adjustment to income, not an itemized deduction.
why.B: Applies 15.3% to the full $80,000 without the 92.35% reduction, then halves it.

why.D: Uses the gross rate on the full profit and deducts all of it.

A penalty on early withdrawal of a certificate of deposit

Her IRA deduction should be $3,750, because she is halfway through the phase-out range
Her IRA deduction should be $7,500, but only if she itemizes
Her IRA deduction should be $0, because her MAGI exceeds the top of the phase-out range for a single taxpayer covered by a workplace plan

why.A: Deductibility depends on whether the taxpayer is covered by a workplace plan and on MAGI.
why.B: The phase-out range ends at $91,000, and her MAGI of $95,000 is above it.
why.C: The IRA deduction is an adjustment to income, available whether or not she itemizes.
why.D: She is covered by an employer plan, and her $95,000 MAGI is above $91,000, so a contribution is not deductible (it may be a nondeductible contribution).

items.law_note: IRA limit $7,500 and deductible IRA phase-out range $81,000-$91,000 (single, covered) confirmed in IRS Notice 2025-67.
items.rule_line: A plan-covered single taxpayer's IRA deduction is zero when MAGI exceeds the top of the phase-out range.

guide.ask: Is Grace covered by an employer plan, and which range applies?
guide.reveal: Yes, so the 81,000 to 91,000 range for a single covered filer applies.

guide.ask: Where does her MAGI of 95,000 fall?
guide.reveal: Above the top of the range, so no deduction is allowed.

items.stem: Compare two homeowners in 2026. Ann bought her main home in 2024 with a $600,000 mortgage. Ben took out a $600,000 home equity loan on his main home in 2024 and used the entire amount to buy a boat and take a vacation. Each paid $36,000 of interest. Which statement is correct?
options: Ann's interest is deductible qualified residence interest; Ben's is not
Both deduct all of the interest, because both loans are secured by a main home
Neither deducts the interest, because personal interest is not deductible in any case
Ann's interest is not deductible; Ben's is, because equity loans are deductible up to $100,000

why.A: Interest on acquisition debt, within the $750,000 limit, is deductible. Home equity debt is qualified only if used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home.
why.B: Being secured by the home is not enough. The debt's use determines whether it is acquisition debt.
why.C: Qualified residence interest is an exception to the personal interest disallowance.
why.D: The $100,000 home equity rule is not current law. Debt used for personal spending is not qualified.

items.law_note: OBBBA (P.L. 119-21) made permanent the rule that home equity debt interest is deductible only if used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home.

guide.ask: When is home mortgage interest deductible?
guide.reveal: On acquisition debt within 750,000, or home equity debt used to buy, build or improve the home.

guide.ask: How do the two homeowners compare?
guide.reveal: Ann's loan bought the home so its interest qualifies; Ben's loan bought a boat and vacation, so his does not.

items.stem: Sandra Kim, a single taxpayer, had a net capital loss of $12,000 for 2026, made up of a $5,000 short-term loss and a $7,000 long-term loss, and had no other capital transactions. How is the loss treated?
options: $12,000 is deductible against ordinary income in 2026
$3,000 is deductible in 2026, and the remaining $9,000 is permanently lost
$3,000 is deductible against ordinary income in 2026, and $9,000 is carried forward indefinitely, retaining its short-term or long-term character
$3,000 is deductible in 2026, and the remaining $9,000 carries forward for only five years

why.A: Deductions of net capital loss against ordinary income are capped at $3,000 ($1,500 if married filing separately).
why.B: The excess is not lost. Individuals carry it forward indefinitely.
why.C: An individual's net capital loss is deductible up to $3,000 per year against ordinary income. Any excess carries forward with no time limit and keeps its character.
why.D: The five-year limit applies to charitable contribution carryforwards, not capital losses. A capital loss carryforward has no expiration for individuals.

items.rule_line: An individual's net capital loss is deductible up to $3,000 per year, with the excess carried forward indefinitely keeping its character.

guide.ask: What is the annual limit on net capital loss against ordinary income?
What happens to the excess and its character?
guide.reveal: 9,000 carries forward indefinitely and keeps its short-term or long-term character.

why.B: The $3,000 limit applies to single filers and joint returns. A married person filing separately is limited to $1,500.
why.C: The limit is not half of the loss. It is a fixed $1,500 for married filing separately.
why.D: There is no rule allowing the full net capital loss against ordinary income.

items.stem: Which taxpayer's rental real estate activities are not automatically treated as passive under the real estate professional rules?
options: Sam, who performed 900 hours in real estate but also works 2,000 hours at a full-time job
Tia, who performed 500 hours in real estate and no other work
Uri, an employee of a real estate firm who owns 2% of it and works there 1,800 hours
Rita, who performed 900 hours of services in real property businesses in which she materially participates, more than half of her 1,600 hours in total of personal services

why.A: His real estate hours are less than half of his total working time.
why.B: She spent all her time in real estate but did not reach the 750-hour minimum.
why.C: Work as an employee counts only if the employee owns more than 5% of the employer.
why.D: To qualify, an individual must spend more than half of her personal service time and more than 750 hours in real property trades or businesses in which she materially participates.

items.rule_line: Real estate professional status requires more than half of personal service time and over 750 hours in real property businesses where she materially participates.

guide.ask: What two tests define a real estate professional?
guide.reveal: More than half of personal service time and more than 750 hours in real property trades in which she materially participates.

guide.ask: Who meets both?
guide.reveal: The person with 900 hours that exceeded half of her 1,600 total; the others fail on hours, time share or ownership.

items.stem: A partner's share of a partnership loss for 2026 exceeds his outside basis in the partnership at year end. How is the excess loss treated?
options: It is not deductible in 2026 and is carried forward indefinitely until the partner has basis to absorb it
It is deductible in 2026 as an ordinary loss, and basis becomes negative
It is converted into a capital loss deductible up to $3,000 per year
It is lost permanently if not used in 2026

why.A: Losses are allowed only to the extent of the partner's basis at year end. The disallowed amount carries forward with no expiration.
why.B: Basis cannot go below zero from losses. The deduction is limited to basis.
why.C: A disallowed partnership loss keeps its character and is not treated as a capital loss.
why.D: The excess carries forward indefinitely and is allowed when basis is restored.

items.rule_line: A partner's loss is allowed only to the extent of outside basis; the excess carries forward indefinitely until basis is restored.

guide.ask: Up to what amount can a partner deduct a partnership loss?
guide.reveal: His outside basis at year end.

guide.ask: What happens to the excess?
guide.reveal: It is not deductible now and carries forward indefinitely until basis exists.

A $9,000 loss on the sale of the taxpayer's main home
A $4,000 loss on the sale of investment stock held for two years
A $1,500 loss on the sale of the taxpayer's furniture used in the home

why.B: A loss on the sale of a personal residence is not deductible.
why.C: Losses on property held for investment are deductible (as capital losses subject to the limits).
why.D: Household furniture is personal-use property, and a loss on its sale is not deductible.

guide.ask: Which losses are deductible for an individual?
guide.reveal: Losses on property held for investment or business, as capital losses subject to limits.

guide.ask: Which listed loss is on investment property?
guide.reveal: The stock held for two years; personal-use property losses are not deductible.

items.stem: Lena sold 100 shares of ABC Corp. at a loss on December 10, 2026. Which of the following purchases would cause her loss to be disallowed under the wash sale rule?
options: A purchase of 100 shares of XYZ Corp., a competitor of ABC, on December 12, 2026
A purchase of 100 shares of ABC Corp. on January 15, 2027
A purchase of 100 shares of ABC Corp. on October 20, 2026
A purchase by her IRA of 100 shares of ABC Corp. on December 27, 2026

why.A: Stock of a different company is not substantially identical, even in the same industry.
why.B: January 15 is 36 days after the sale, outside the 61-day window.
why.C: October 20 is 51 days before the sale, outside the window that starts 30 days before.
why.D: A purchase of substantially identical stock within 30 days before or after the sale, including a purchase by the taxpayer's IRA, triggers the wash sale rule.

items.rule_line: A wash sale arises from buying substantially identical stock, including by the taxpayer's IRA, within 30 days before or after the sale.

guide.ask: What does the wash sale rule cover?
guide.reveal: A purchase of substantially identical stock within 30 days before or after the loss sale.

guide.ask: Which listed purchase falls in the window and involves the same stock?
guide.reveal: A purchase by her IRA of ABC shares on December 27; a different company, a date beyond 30 days, or a purchase 30 days later than the window are out.

items.stem: Bill breeds racehorses as a hobby with no profit motive. In 2026 the activity produced $8,000 of income and $12,000 of expenses. How is the activity treated for the year?
options: The $8,000 is included in gross income, and the $12,000 of expenses is not deductible
Bill reports a $4,000 loss from the activity on Schedule C
The $8,000 is excluded from gross income because it is a hobby
The $8,000 is included, and $8,000 of expenses is deductible as an itemized deduction

why.A: Hobby income is taxable, but hobby expenses are miscellaneous itemized deductions, which are not allowed, so no loss arises.
why.B: A hobby cannot generate a loss. The activity is not a trade or business.
why.C: Income from a hobby is taxable.
why.D: Before 2018 hobby expenses were deductible up to income as itemized deductions. They are not deductible now.

guide.ask: Is hobby income taxable?
guide.reveal: Yes, 8,000 is included.

guide.ask: Are hobby expenses deductible?
guide.reveal: No, they are miscellaneous itemized deductions that are not allowed, so no loss arises.

why.C: Reports the net loss ($6,000) as the carryforward without deducting the $3,000 used in 2026.
why.D: Ignores the $4,000 gain and the $3,000 deduction.

steps: Net = 10,000 ST loss - 4,000 LT gain = 6,000 net loss

why.B: Losses are limited first by outside basis ($60,000) and then by the amount at risk ($50,000). Adam deducts $50,000, and $20,000 is carried forward.
why.C: Applies only the basis limitation and ignores the at-risk limit.
why.D: Deducts the entire loss, ignoring both limits.

why.C: This is the disallowed portion, not the allowed loss.
why.D: Deducts the full loss and ignores the wash sale on the 60 replacement shares.

items.stem: Cara Bell sold stock with a $20,000 basis to her brother for $14,000 in 2026, its fair market value. In 2027 the brother sold the same stock to an unrelated buyer for $24,000. What gain does the brother recognize in 2027?

why.A: Treats the whole gain as eliminated. The brother reduces his gain only by the $6,000 loss that Cara could not deduct, leaving $4,000.
why.B: Cara's $6,000 loss on the sale to a related person is disallowed. Her brother's basis is his $14,000 cost, and on his later sale he may reduce his $10,000 gain by the disallowed loss: $4,000.
why.C: This is Cara's disallowed loss, not the brother's gain.
why.D: Ignores the reduction for the disallowed loss.

items.rule_line: A loss on a sale to a related person is disallowed, but the buyer may reduce later gain by that disallowed loss.

guide.ask: Is the sister's loss on a sale to a related person allowed?
guide.reveal: No, the 6,000 loss is disallowed.

guide.ask: What is the brother's realized gain on his later sale?
How is it reduced?
guide.reveal: By the disallowed 6,000 loss, so 10,000 - 6,000 = 4,000 recognized.

items.stem: Nolan Pierce has a net operating loss carryforward of $100,000 from 2025. His 2026 taxable income before the NOL deduction is $70,000. What is his NOL deduction for 2026, and what NOL remains?
options: A $70,000 deduction, with $30,000 remaining to carry forward
A $100,000 deduction, with no NOL remaining
A $56,000 deduction, with $44,000 remaining to carry forward
A $56,000 deduction, with the remaining $44,000 lost

why.A: Deducts 100% of taxable income. The post-2017 NOL deduction is limited to 80%.
why.B: The NOL deduction cannot exceed 80% of taxable income before the NOL deduction.
why.C: For NOLs arising after 2017, the deduction is limited to 80% of taxable income before the NOL: 80% x $70,000 = $56,000. The remaining $44,000 carries forward indefinitely.
why.D: The excess carries forward indefinitely for NOLs arising after 2017.

items.rule_line: For NOLs arising after 2017, the deduction is limited to 80% of taxable income, with the excess carried forward indefinitely.

guide.ask: What limit applies to post-2017 NOL deductions?
guide.reveal: 80% of taxable income before the NOL.

guide.ask: What is the deduction?
What remains?
guide.reveal: 100,000 - 56,000 = 44,000, carried forward indefinitely.

items.stem: Tom Ruiz is single and has a 2026 loss of $300,000 from a sole proprietorship that is his only business. He also earned $400,000 of wages. Assume the 2026 excess business loss threshold for a single filer is $256,000. What business loss may Tom deduct in 2026, and what happens to the rest?
options: $300,000 is deductible because his wages exceed the loss
$44,000 is deductible, and $256,000 is carried forward
$256,000 is deductible, and the $44,000 excess is lost
$256,000 is deductible, and the $44,000 excess is carried forward as an NOL

why.A: Wages do not allow additional business losses. The threshold applies to net business losses.
why.B: Reverses the amounts. The threshold is the amount that may be deducted.
why.C: The disallowed excess is carried forward as a net operating loss, not lost.
why.D: The excess business loss limit disallows business losses above the threshold. The disallowed amount is treated as an NOL carryforward.

items.law_note: OBBBA (P.L. 119-21) made the excess business loss limitation permanent (it had been scheduled to expire after 2028). The threshold is inflation-adjusted; the stem supplies $256,000. Testable from 2026-07-01.
items.testable_basis: OBBBA provision effective 2024/2025: AICPA Board of Examiners policy (2025-09-18) -> testable 2026-07-01
items.rule_line: Excess business losses above the threshold are disallowed and carried forward as an NOL.

guide.ask: What does the excess business loss limit do?
guide.reveal: Disallows business losses above the threshold, here 256,000.

guide.ask: How much is disallowed and how is it treated?
guide.reveal: 300,000 - 256,000 = 44,000, carried forward as an NOL.

Treating Shawn's business loss as a negative amount of income and ignoring all other items, by how much does the income Tara includes from the activity exceed Shawn's result?

why.A: This is only Shawn's loss and ignores Tara's inclusion.
why.B: Compares only Tara's inclusion and omits Shawn's loss deduction.

why.D: Adds all revenue and expenses. The difference is between the two net results.

items.stem: Two single taxpayers each lose $70,000 on stock that becomes worthless in 2026 and each has no other capital transactions. Vic's stock qualifies as small business stock eligible for ordinary loss treatment and was originally issued to him for money. Wade's stock is ordinary stock. What is the difference between Vic's and Wade's total loss deductions against ordinary income in 2026?

why.A: Uses the capital loss portion of Vic's loss as the difference.
why.B: Vic deducts $50,000 as an ordinary loss and the remaining $20,000 as a capital loss limited to $3,000: $53,000. Wade's capital loss is limited to $3,000. Difference: $50,000.
why.C: This is Vic's total deduction, not the difference from Wade's.
why.D: Assumes Vic can deduct all $70,000 as an ordinary loss. The ordinary limit for a single filer is $50,000.

guide.ask: How much of Vic's loss is ordinary?
guide.reveal: 50,000, the ordinary loss limit for a single filer on eligible small business stock.

items.task: Review Form 1040 and supporting documentation to determine accuracy of losses reported.
items.stem: Zoe Marsh is a limited partner in a partnership (a passive activity for her). At the end of 2026 her outside basis is $40,000 and her at-risk amount is $30,000, before the current-year loss. Her share of the partnership's 2026 loss is $45,000. She also has $12,000 of passive income from a different passive investment. Applying the loss limitations in the proper order, what loss may she deduct in 2026?

why.A: The loss passes the basis limit ($40,000) and at-risk limit ($30,000), and the passive activity limit then allows the loss only to the extent of passive income ($12,000).
why.B: Stops after the at-risk limit and ignores the passive activity rules.
why.C: Applies only the basis limitation.
why.D: Deducts the entire loss without applying basis, at-risk, or passive limits.

items.rule_line: Loss limits apply in order: basis, at-risk, then passive activity, which allows losses up to passive income.

guide.ask: What is the deduction after the basis limit?
What follows after the at-risk limit?
What does the passive limit allow?
guide.reveal: Only passive income, min(30,000, 12,000) = 12,000.

items.task: Calculate losses disallowed for tax purposes, such as from a hobby, wash sale or sale of a personal-use asset.
items.stem: Compare two taxpayers who each sold stock at a $5,000 loss on December 10, 2026, and bought identical replacement stock on December 20, 2026. Kim bought the replacement stock in her taxable brokerage account. Lee's IRA bought the replacement stock. Which statement is correct?
options: Both losses are disallowed; Kim adds the loss to the basis of the replacement stock, but Lee's disallowed loss is not added to his IRA basis
Kim's loss is disallowed and Lee's loss is allowed, because an IRA is a separate taxpayer
Both losses are allowed, because a wash sale requires the same account to buy the stock
Both losses are disallowed and both add the disallowed loss to the basis of the replacement stock

why.A: The wash sale rule applies to purchases by the taxpayer's IRA as well, but the disallowed loss cannot be added to IRA basis, so it is permanently lost.
why.B: The IRS treats a purchase by the taxpayer's own IRA as a wash sale. The IRA is not a separate taxpayer for this purpose.
why.C: The rule does not depend on the account. Purchases by the taxpayer, spouse, or IRA can trigger it.
why.D: Basis of an IRA investment does not increase for the disallowed loss, so Lee cannot recover it.

items.rule_line: The wash sale rule applies to IRA purchases, but the disallowed loss cannot be added to IRA basis and is lost.

guide.ask: Does a wash sale apply to a purchase by the taxpayer's IRA?
guide.reveal: Yes, the loss is disallowed for both.

guide.ask: Where does the disallowed loss go for each account?
guide.reveal: It adds to the replacement stock basis in the taxable account but cannot add to IRA basis, so it is lost.

why.C: Deducts the full carryforward. The 80% limit reduces the deduction to $80,000.
why.D: Deducts all taxable income, which the 80% limit prevents.

Which is smaller, that or the 90,000 carryforward?

Compare filing a joint return with filing separate returns. What is the difference between the combined amount added to (or subtracted from) taxable income from these capital transactions on separate returns, and on a joint return?

why.B: Uses only the joint return net loss and ignores the separate return results.
why.C: On a joint return the amounts are netted: $8,000 - $10,000 = $2,000 net loss, fully deductible. Separately, Alex deducts $1,500 and Bea reports $8,000, for a net $6,500 of income. The separate-return result is $8,500 higher.
why.D: Uses the loss amount and ignores that netting on a joint return offsets the gain.

guide.reveal: 8,000 - 10,000 = a 2,000 net loss, fully deductible.

guide.ask: What is the difference?

why.D: A child under age 24 who is a full-time student, lives with the taxpayer for more than half the year, and does not provide more than half of his own support is a qualifying child.

The former husband may claim the child tax credit and file as head of household because of the son
Pia loses head of household status because she released her claim to the child
The release is invalid unless it is attached by the custodial parent for each future year

items.stem: Eli Grant, a single taxpayer with MAGI far above $200,000, sold all his S corporation stock in 2026 and realized a $200,000 gain. The S corporation's assets included active business assets and investment assets. If the corporation had sold all its assets at fair market value on the sale date, $20,000 of gain would be from investment assets, and $180,000 would be from active trade or business assets in which Eli materially participates. What is Eli's net investment income tax on the stock gain?

why.A: Gain on a disposition of S corporation stock is net investment income only to the extent of the net gain that would be taken into account on a deemed asset sale of the passive assets: $20,000. Tax = 3.8% x $20,000 = $760.
why.B: Taxes half of the stock gain. The taxable part is the gain on the investment assets in the deemed asset sale ($20,000).
why.C: Taxes the gain attributable to the active business assets, which is excluded.
why.D: Treats the entire stock gain as investment income.

steps: Deemed sale gain from investment assets = 20,000
